How do we get to plug-and-play robots?

Community Article Published
October 30, 2026 Upvote 5 Luca Cilio lucakae projectsim
At Long Horizon in San Francisco, I listened to Felipe Chavez Cortes, co-founder and CEO of Robot.com, talk about what it takes to deploy a robot. One of his slides compared policies running as is with systems that added planning, memory, outcome checks or safety mechanisms around them.
A simple summary of the talk would be: even with a generalist model as the starting point, there is still so much manual work around fine-tuning, testing, integration and system engineering before the robot can be deployed.
Reading the papers behind the talk, alongside the recent generalist-model releases, made me wonder how much of that work will still fall to the team deploying the robot. Policies are carrying more knowledge into unfamiliar situations, while AI agents are beginning to take on some of the diagnosis and experimentation that engineers do today. Progress in both directions brings us closer to plug-and-play robot systems. It also raises a question for the labs building them: how do we give those models enough experience, and test them thoroughly enough, before asking customers to rely on them?

The work between a policy and a deployment

Some of that manual work goes into something that sounds simple: deciding when an action is finished. VoLo combines π0.5 with a vision-language model that plans and monitors execution, plus grasp and placement tools. In its hardware evaluation, the full system completed 18 of 42 trials across 14 tasks, compared with 6 of 42 for the standalone policy. That is a substantial improvement, although it still leaves more than half the trials unsuccessful.
One of the paper's simulated failures shows why checking the outcome is a problem of its own. The monitor concludes that an orange is in a white bowl while the orange is still on the table. The system has a mechanism for checking progress, but the answer it receives is wrong.

The monitor reports that the orange is in the white bowl. The orange is still on the table. Image from the VoLo paper, showing a simulated trial.
This is where keeping track of the scene can help. POT-VLA maintains persistent 3D records of task objects, using them both to guide actions and to check relations such as whether one object is inside another. When an object becomes occluded, the system keeps track of the uncertainty and can request another observation. The policy is also fine-tuned to use this information, so improving the outcome check involves changes to both the controller and the information available to it.
Even a correctly executed action can leave the robot stuck, though. In a simulated example from BATON, a top grasp lifts a can successfully, but the combined height of the can and gripper prevents placement inside a microwave. A side grasp works. The grasp has to serve the placement, which is why BATON records constraints on skills and their transitions: the next operation needs to influence the choice the robot makes now.
For that coordination to work, the policy must reliably follow the planner's instructions. Tool-Aligned VLA post-trains policies to execute bounded subtasks, follow precise instructions and report progress. In several of its simulated comparisons, putting a planner above a conventionally trained policy actually reduced success. Training the executor for the way it would be called helped the two work together.
These are some of the decisions a deployment team has to get right: what the robot remembers, how its actions fit together, and what evidence allows it to move on. A model with a large repertoire of skills helps enormously, but the team still needs to turn that repertoire into a system that completes the job.

What is beginning to carry over

The encouraging change is how much learned competence can now carry over to a new setting. In Figure's Helix 2.5 evaluation, three behaviours—tidying, towel folding and bedmaking—were each fine-tuned on task data collected elsewhere, then tested in 30 unseen homes with unseen objects. Each task used one fixed checkpoint across the homes. With the task data, architecture and training procedure held constant, pretraining on Figure's Index human dataset raised full-task completion from 9% to 56%. The tasks had been taught, but teaching them did not have to start again in every home.
Something similar is happening across robot hardware. PI's π0.7 folds laundry with a dual-arm UR5e setup despite having no laundry demonstrations for that robot. The robot was present in training on other tasks. The result brings together knowledge about the embodiment and about folding without demonstrations of that particular robot-task combination.
When the task itself changes, the question becomes how much new experience is needed. Generalist's GEN-1.5 accepts physical demonstrations as prompts: sensor observations and action trajectories recorded with handheld grippers or a robot. Across ten short tasks, one 3–12 second demonstration produced 59% average success without gradient updates. Five minutes of data per task and ten fine-tuning steps produced 83%. Both the data budget and adaptation method changed, but the small amount of task-specific experience is what makes these results interesting.

Two adaptation settings across ten short tasks. Chart based on Generalist's reported results; whiskers show the reported standard deviations.
Skild's S1 uses an egocentric video of a person performing the task. Its selected demonstrations include plant potting, pancake preparation and kit assembly, with tasks lasting up to ten minutes that the company reports were absent from training. These longer sequences suggest how a demonstration can communicate the organisation of a job, drawing on skills the robot has already learned.
In these prompting results, a demonstration can specify a job using skills the model already has. That makes a few seconds of task-specific data useful, while leaving the result dependent on a much larger body of prior learning.

Generalist demonstrates physical prompting and adaptation with GEN-1.5.
The remaining difficulty is what happens when the robot tries the task and fails. A demonstration may communicate the intended sequence perfectly without explaining why the can will not fit through the microwave opening. Someone still has to diagnose the problem and find a change that works.

Adaptation can itself become a capability

Some of the research is beginning to put that responsibility on AI systems. In Recursive Harness Distillation, a more capable agent experiments with policy interventions and writes a playbook for a lighter agent. The playbook is refined using the lighter agent's execution. One illustrated revision develops a simple retry instruction into guidance to inspect a failed grasp, check the contact between object and fingers, and verify that the object follows the gripper. The result is reusable guidance for handling a failure that might otherwise require an engineer's attention.
Google's Gemini 4 Argon robotics demonstrations take on more of this preparation. In one example, the model constructs an articulated MuJoCo twin of a foot-pedal bin, practises balance and pedal stepping, then controls a Spot robot to dispose of a can. It uses an existing manipulation skill and explicit instructions to verify foot and hand alignment. A separate example has it inspect logs and video of a simple arm's pick-and-place attempts, test fixes and retry.
These are curated demonstrations with substantial instructions and tooling, but they show parts of the work from the deployment talk becoming things a model can do: inspecting an attempt, proposing a change and trying it. A stronger underlying policy gives this process more to work with. The fix may be a different grasp or subgoal, rather than an entirely new manipulation skill.
Finding that fix can still be hard. The last few failures may be precisely the ones the system cannot diagnose, and the orange on the table is a reminder that a confident explanation can be wrong. The system needs experience to learn from and a way to check whether its changes actually help.

The experience has to come from somewhere

That need begins long before deployment. The transfer results above depend on a model having already learned enough to handle a new room, robot or instruction. A lab trying to build that competence needs many more interactions than any one customer will ever see.
Collecting them physically means paying for robot time, operators and resets, with each new arrangement requiring another attempt. Simulation lets a team run many copies of a task, change the starting conditions and generate experience in parallel. For a task like the microwave example, that could mean practising across different can positions, openings and grasp choices before the policy reaches a real kitchen.
NVIDIA’s work on synthetic training data gives a sense of the volume simulation can provide. For GR00T N1, NVIDIA reports generating 780,000 simulated trajectories in 11 hours using DexMimicGen, covering 6,500 hours of trajectory time across its pre- and post-training datasets. The process transforms and replays segments of human demonstrations in new configurations, retaining successful attempts. Human examples still supply the behaviour; simulation expands the experience that can be built from them.

GR00T N1 combines several sources of experience. Its synthetic data includes both physics-simulated trajectories and generated videos. Figure from the GR00T N1 paper.
More experience also creates more choices: different datasets, training methods and checkpoints can all produce different policies. A lab needs to know which of those changes actually improves the robot. As the policy covers more tasks, testing every version on hardware becomes an increasingly expensive way to find out.
Simulation allows those versions to face the same held-out situations, repeatedly, while varying particular conditions to find where performance breaks down. In SIMPLER, simulated rollouts tracked real-world policy rankings more closely than action-prediction error on recorded demonstrations did on the tested Google Robot tasks. The robot's behaviour during execution revealed something that predicting actions in a dataset did not.
Those evaluations can then guide the next round of training. If a policy struggles with a particular placement or object arrangement, the team has a concrete target for additional experience and a test to run again afterwards. When a new deployment exposes another gap, the same process can extend to it. In some cases, simulation can supply the task example itself: GEN-1.5 used simulated rollouts as prompts for a real robot on a subset of tasks, without another training run. Experience from simulation could guide the action directly, as well as provide data for updating the policy.
Training, evaluation and adaptation are connected by this repeated use of experience: learning from it, testing what was learned, and finding what is still missing. Simulation can support that process while the foundation model is being built, while a team prepares it for a job, and as new failures appear.

The simulation has to preserve the difficulty

There is a condition on all of this: the simulated task must teach or test something that carries over to the real one. If the fingers pass through the microwave opening, or unrealistic friction keeps the can attached to the gripper, generating more attempts only reinforces the wrong lesson.
The same problem can invalidate an evaluation. In SIMPLER, replaying a real robot's actions initially produced a missed grasp in simulation. Calibrating the simulated controller made it track the real motion more closely and reproduce the grasp. Without that correction, a team could mistake a simulator error for a weakness in the policy.

Real execution on the left; simulated replay before and after controller calibration in the middle and on the right. The action sequence is the same. Figure from SIMPLER.
This is why useful simulation requires more than an attractive reconstruction. Geometry, appearance, articulation and physical properties determine what the robot sees and what its actions do. Which details need the most care depends on the task: clearance is central to the microwave example, while the can-pickup comparison exposes the importance of matching the controller's response. Real-robot checks establish which conclusions from simulation deserve to be trusted.
Creating those environments is itself a substantial part of the work. If every new task requires weeks of manual construction and calibration, simulation inherits the scaling problem it is supposed to help solve. Teams need to be able to build, vary and reuse interactive tasks without rebuilding the entire experiment each time.

How plug-and-play could arrive

The prospect that makes this research exciting is how much more of the preparation could carry into the next deployment. A foundation model can bring a larger repertoire of skills. Broad evaluation can uncover weaknesses before a customer encounters them. And an AI system can help work out what a particular job still requires. The customer may see a robot that gets to work quickly because a great deal of learning and testing has already happened elsewhere.
The measure of progress is whether this preparation produces robots that handle more jobs reliably, with less specialist effort for each new one.
This is what we are building towards with projectsim. The assets and scenes are the starting point; we want to turn them into simulations where teams can run policies, generate useful experience and understand how their robots behave. A team should be able to reuse an environment, vary its tasks and test a new policy without starting the simulation work again. Making that practical would give robotics labs more room to pursue the learning and testing that make the next deployment easier.
